cards.explanation: The answer is the Spirit of God. Pharaoh asks, “Can we find anyone like this man, in whom the Spirit of God abides?” That's the king of Egypt putting it to his officials out loud. They had just been pleased with the proposal (v. 37). When a king says that about you, your résumé is done.

The answer is the throne. Pharaoh says, “Only with regard to the throne will I be greater than you.” He puts Joseph over his house and tells all his people to obey Joseph's commands. The one place he stays above Joseph is the throne, the king's own place. A boss can hand off nearly everything and still keep the name on the door.

The answer is garments of fine linen, friends. Pharaoh “…clothed him in garments of fine linen…” Joseph walks in with a plan and comes out dressed for the job. Me? I own one outfit, a white apron, and it's had flour on it since day one.

The answer is True. The text says Pharaoh “…placed a gold chain around his neck.” That's the signet ring, the fine linen and now a gold chain. By the time Pharaoh finishes, Joseph is carrying more gear than I ever got out of that junk drawer I used to live in.

The answer is “Bow the knee!” The text says Joseph rode in Pharaoh's second chariot, with men calling out before him, “Bow the knee!” Then it says Pharaoh placed him over all the land of Egypt. That's a loud way to start a new job.

The answer is a wife. Pharaoh “…gave him Asenath daughter of Potiphera, priest of On, to be his wife.” That comes right after the new name, Zaphenath-paneah. So Joseph got a new name and a wife in the same verse. Some people spend years on one of those.

The answer is thirty. The text says, “…Joseph was thirty years old when he entered the service of Pharaoh king of Egypt.” Earlier, the writer tells us he was seventeen (Genesis 37:2), so the Bible gives us both ages. I spent a long stretch in a junk drawer, and the only thing anybody handed me was dust. Joseph got a whole land to take charge of.

The answer is fields, friends. The text says, “In every city he laid up the food from the fields around it.” Each city's food came from its own surrounding fields. It's like keeping a cookie jar in every room instead of one jar at the far end of the house.

The answer is False. Joseph did not keep an exact count, because he “…stopped keeping track of it…” The grain was “…like the sand of the sea…” and the text says “…it was beyond measure.” That's how much there was. Even the man doing the storing couldn't keep up with the count.

The answer is forget all his hardship. Joseph says, “God has made me forget all my hardship and all my father’s household.” That's the name he gives his firstborn, Manasseh. Joseph credits God, not himself. The hardship was real, and I think this name is how he talks about it.

The answer is True. Joseph says, “God has made me fruitful in the land of my affliction.” That's the name he gives his second son, Ephraim. Joseph calls Egypt the land of his affliction, and he says God made him fruitful there.
The answer is Joseph. The famine began “…just as Joseph had said.” He told Pharaoh about seven years of abundance and then seven years of famine (Genesis 41:29-30). And here it was, right on time.

The answer is food. The text says, “…although there was famine in every country, there was food throughout the land of Egypt.” Every other country was in famine, but Egypt had food. That's because of the storehouses Joseph filled.

The answer is “Go to Joseph and do whatever he tells you.” The people cried out to Pharaoh for food, and his answer was short. He told all the Egyptians, “Go to Joseph and do whatever he tells you.” Earlier in the passage, Pharaoh placed Joseph over all the land of Egypt (v. 41), and now the people hear it in plain words. That's a clear chain of command.

The answer is False, friends. Joseph “…opened up all the storehouses and sold grain to the Egyptians…” The text says sold, not gave. The famine was severe in the land of Egypt, and the grain went out as a sale.

The answer is every nation. The text says, “…every nation came to Joseph in Egypt to buy grain…” The famine was severe over all the earth, so they all came. That's one man with one storehouse system and a line out the door. Not a small job.
